rv.q: 'Paradise Square' is the kind of new musical that Broadway needs more of: an original story that is ambitious, moving and entertaining, with a diverse cast singing in formidable harmony.

Clarified, intensified and inestimably improved since its less-cohesive Chicago tryout, 'Paradise Square' focuses on how poor Irish immigrants shared a neighborhood with Black Americans, intermarrying, exchanging cultures and sharing music and dance.
It’s the kind of moment that sends electricity up and down your spine as it takes place.
The problem is that the writing doesn't support the spectacle, yielding a ponderous hash of good intentions that often feels like a training-wheels version of Ragtime.
And somewhere along the line it reaches a point of no return, when all that reaching just wears itself out.
Racism becomes an individual character flaw instead of a systemic evil; resistance, the solitary moral genius of a hero.

The new musical 'Paradise Square' has ambitions as grand as its sprawling cast and period setting, but despite moments of genuine power, it never quite coheres into the unified artistic statement it strives to be.
The disappointment on this evening is in trying to say it all.
It makes the virtuosic Black dancers seem unmusical — but really it’s the musical itself failing to listen.
Joaquina Kalukango whose memorable performance is certain to go down in the record books and be a top contender for the Tony Award makes this a must-see show.
Paradise Square is an ambitious musical that tackles issues of race, class, and immigration in Civil War-era New York with impressive performances and stunning choreography.
The resilience demonstrated by Kalukango’s character and others in Paradise Square seems fitting in a show that might have been prematurely written off as the latest big musical that couldn’t.
Is this the next Phantom or Les Miserables?
Book by Christina Anderson, Craig Lucas, and Larry Kirwan. Lyrics by Nathan Tysen and Masi Asare. Additional music by Larry Kirwan, inspired in part by the songs of Stephen Foster.
Ultimately, there are just too many proverbial “round holes” to comfortably fit into this “Square” peg!
Challenging, adult shows like this are always welcome but, having gone through a lengthy development process, its overcrowded book still needs sorting out.
The performances under his direction are scattered all over the Broadway map, from Kalukango’s star-making turn to Dossett’s understated villain to Kennedy’s brassy performance.
And yet, without a story line to guide us, and songs that do not further the tale, in the end we are left wandering in the wilderness holding a bowlful of good intentions.
Paradise Square is a musical that wears its good intentions on its sleeve, but those intentions don't always translate into compelling theater.
The mechanics of the show work against it.
Paradise Square is a show that wants to be everything to everyone, and in trying to do so, it ends up being not quite enough for anyone.
But “Paradise Square” was largely a disappointment.
Unfortunately, she cannot singlehandedly save a Broadway musical suffering from an identity crisis.
Although well-meaning and filled with some striking visuals and pointed political commentary, “Paradise Square” is sappy, overstuffed, overlong, and tiresome.
I felt irresistibly drawn to these characters, constantly striving for something better even when the hand they were dealt said it wasn't in the cards.
His work, since he arrived on these shores, has enriched New York and the debut on Broadway of his “Paradise Square” is just what the theater needs to regain its glorious past.
At its best, that variety of contributors have made for a rich, dialectical depiction of a complex slice of history.
Paradise Square may not be a great musical, but it is certainly not bad either.
The company is continually immersed in song and movement, and the result is a vibrant tableau of a dynamic time in our history.
Neither Paradise Square nor Suffs is truly bad. But neither is as rewarding as it might have been either.

cn.t: An ambitious but overstuffed musical about Civil War-era New York that features powerhouse performances (especially Joaquina Kalukango) and stunning choreography, though critics found the sprawling story unfocused and exhausting.
